spots.name: Quba Mosque
spots.label: Quba Mosque

text.geographic_location: In the Quba district of Medina, in the Hejaz region of Saudi Arabia. It was once a separate village outside the city, which Medina has since grown to include.
text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements and any access limits.
text.directions_text: Head to Quba Mosque in Medina. From there it is about 1 minute on foot to the mosque, heading west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description:
Quba Mosque is thought to be the first mosque in the world, first built in the 7th century during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad. Tradition says he laid its first stone when he stopped at the village of Quba' on his journey to Medina. The building you see today dates from a complete reconstruction begun in 1984 and inaugurated on 2 November 1986. It was designed by the Egyptian architect Abdel-Wahed El-Wakil in a traditional style and has four minarets and 56 domes. That gives you a lot of repeating shapes to work with: rows of small domes, tall slim towers and a pale, even-toned building.

The mosque stands in a large plot of about 13,500 square metres, so it is easiest to photograph from a little distance. Pick a moment when fewer people are in front of you. Keep the minarets upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little sky above them. A larger expansion of the mosque and its surroundings was announced in 2022, so what you see around it may change from visit to visit.

This is a working place of worship, so be discreet around people at prayer and avoid pointing your phone at worshippers.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a minaret with a vertical line so it stands straight. Put the horizon on the lower third and leave some sky above. For a second shot, zoom in on the row of domes. Step back a little rather than tilting the phone upwards, which makes the towers lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit this view, as the sun should be behind you and light the face of the mosque. Late afternoon is a good second choice if you want softer light.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the mosque in its setting. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole building will not fit, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the light stonework keeps its detail. Do not use portrait mode for the building. Panorama can work if you stand still and pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front courtyard, facing the domes and minarets). The white domes and minarets framed from the open courtyard, with the wide-angle view taking in the whole building. From here the mosque sits in front of you with its minarets and domes in view.

spots.alt: Quba Mosque, Medina: thought to be the first mosque in the world. Photo spot

text.access_note: This is a major place of worship and pilgrimage, and rules about who may enter, what to wear and where photography is allowed can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the centre of Medina, the area around the Prophet's Mosque; no stations or tram stops are listed for this spot. Then find the phone icon on the map. From there the middle of the mosque is about 143 m to the north, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
The Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawī) stands at the heart of Medina. It is the second mosque built by the Prophet Muhammad in the city, after Quba Mosque. It is also the second largest mosque, and the second holiest site in Islam after the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca. The first building dates from 622 and was far smaller than today's. It began as an open-air space used as a community centre, a court and a religious school. Later rulers expanded and decorated it again and again, so what you see now is the result of many centuries of building. The mosque also contains the graves of Muhammad and the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar. Its best-known feature is the Green Dome, at the south-east corner. In 1909 it became the first place in the Arabian Peninsula to have electric lights.

The mosque photographs well because of its sheer scale, its minarets and the contrast of the green dome against pale stonework. It is too big to fit in one frame from close up, so choose what the picture is about: the long frontage, a single minaret, or the dome. Keep your phone straight and use the gridlines so the walls and towers don't lean. Be considerate of worshippers, and avoid pointing the camera at people who are praying.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a minaret or wall edge with a vertical line so it stays upright. Leave some sky above the towers. For the Green Dome, zoom in and let the dome fill the middle of the frame rather than shrinking it among the buildings. If the ultra-wide stretches the edges, move back a little if you can, or use the default lens (1x) and take two shots of different parts.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft and the surroundings are quieter, or after sunset when the mosque is lit. Prayer times are busiest, so expect more people then.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the mosque. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a section of it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Green Dome and the tops of the minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white walls keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid, like a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The mosque is very large, so you will be seeing one part of it rather than all of it.

spots.name: Islamic University of Madinah
spots.label: Islamic University

text.geographic_location: In the Medina area of Saudi Arabia.
text.access_note: The gate and public frontage can be photographed from outside, but administrative areas, classrooms and student residences need university permits, so check the university's official site before you go.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so travel from central Medina to the Islamic University's main gate. Ask for the main gate on the city side. Once there, walk along the public frontage rather than into the campus. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: The Islamic University of Madinah is a public Islamic university in Medina, founded by royal decree in 1961. It began with Islamic studies and now also teaches Arabic, law, business, computing, engineering and the sciences. For a visitor with a phone, the best-looking part of it is the main entrance: a monumental gateway that faces the city, so the approach from the city side gives a clean, straight-on view. The gate photographs well because it is big, symmetrical and easy to read, and you can take it from the public side without going into the campus. Stand back far enough to fit the whole portal in, and keep the frame level so the sides of the gateway don't lean. For a quieter, more open angle, Islamic University Square shows the campus frontage and the valley setting. Keep to the public perimeter: administrative areas, classrooms and student residences need university permits. Photography is generally fine in public areas, but be discreet and ask before photographing anywhere sensitive. Avoid pointing your phone at students or staff without asking.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the gateway up with the middle of the frame. Keep the phone upright and level so the sides of the portal stay straight. Leave some road or forecourt in the foreground to give a sense of approach. For a quieter, more open alternative, try Islamic University Square, which shows the campus frontage and the valley setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gateway than the middle of the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the gateway. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the whole portal in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for tighter framing of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the gate keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case vehicles or people pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The campus lies to the east, beyond the gate.

spots.alt: Islamic University of Madinah, Medina: a public Islamic university. Photo spot
